Name: epistemic_certainty_transfer
Title: Knowing vs. Saying: Is a Multilingual LLM's Internal 'I Know This' Signal Language-Agnostic, and Can It Rescue Facts the Model Knows But Fails to Express?
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs possess a largely language-agnostic internal 'epistemic certainty' representation (whether the model knows a fact) that is partially decoupled from language-specific expression machinery. Consequently, many cross-lingual factual failures are not knowledge gaps but access/expression failures: the model internally 'knows' a fact (its shared certainty signal is high and the correct answer is decodable in intermediate layers) yet produces a wrong or low-confidence surface answer in the query language. We hypothesize (1) a single low-rank certainty direction, trained on one language, linearly predicts factual correctness across all other languages far above chance; (2) a substantial fraction of wrong non-English answers are 'known-but-unexpressed' (correct answer recoverable via cross-lingual logit-lens/PatchScopes despite wrong surface output); and (3) steering along the shared certainty direction plus a language-alignment vector recovers these known-but-unexpressed facts, improving low-resource accuracy without new knowledge.
Related Work: Prior calibration work (Ahuja et al. 2022 on MMLM calibration; C3; N2C2) studies output-probability calibration for classification and proposes cascades/kNN fixes, treating confidence as a scalar to be recalibrated. Cross-lingual consistency and self-alignment work (CALM, RankC, X-KDE) treats disagreement as inconsistency to be trained away via DPO/editing. Interpretability work finds shared vs. language-specific neurons and 'known/unknown' probes (in English). What is missing: a mechanistic test of whether the *internal epistemic-certainty representation* is language-agnostic and separable from expression, and whether cross-lingual failures are frequently expression failures over knowable facts. We move from output-level recalibration and consistency training to a mechanistic 'knowing vs. saying' distinction, quantifying a known-but-unexpressed gap and providing a training-free, direction-based repair. This is novel relative to both the calibration literature and my prior interference/pivot/cultural/fragmentation proposals.
Abstract: Multilingual LLMs answer factual questions correctly in English far more often than in lower-resource languages. This is usually attributed to missing knowledge in those languages. We argue that a large share of these failures are instead expression failures: the model internally 'knows' the fact but cannot surface it in the query language. We investigate whether multilingual LLMs carry a language-agnostic internal 'epistemic certainty' signal—a representation of whether they know a fact—that is partially decoupled from the language-specific machinery that produces the answer. First, we train a linear probe to predict per-fact correctness from intermediate residual-stream activations on a single source language and test whether it transfers zero-shot to predict correctness across ten typologically diverse languages, indicating a shared certainty subspace. Second, we quantify a 'known-but-unexpressed' gap: for questions answered incorrectly in a target language, we test whether the correct answer is nonetheless decodable from intermediate layers via cross-lingual logit-lens and PatchScopes, and whether the shared certainty probe fires high. Third, we introduce a training-free repair that combines steering along the shared certainty direction with a language-alignment vector to recover these facts. Across four open models and a Wikidata-derived multilingual fact set, we report probe cross-lingual transfer AUC, the size of the known-but-unexpressed gap per language and language distance, and accuracy gains from repair with specificity controls. This reframes multilingual factual gaps as partly a controllable knowing-vs-saying problem.
Experiments: 1) Fact set: ~1500 subject-relation-object triples from Wikidata rendered as parallel cloze/QA prompts in 10 languages (English, German, Spanish, French, Russian, Hindi, Arabic, Chinese, Japanese, Swahili) with template generation + MT/native verification. Record entity popularity as a confound covariate. 2) Correctness labels: for open models (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Aya-23-8B, Gemma-2-9B), compute per-(fact,language) correctness via answer normalization/first-token matching, plus surface confidence (answer token probability). 3) Shared certainty probe: extract mid-layer residual activations at the last prompt token; train a linear/logistic probe to predict correctness using ONLY English (or one source-language) data; evaluate zero-shot on all target languages (report per-language AUC vs. an in-language-trained ceiling and a chance baseline). Do reciprocal source-language sweeps to test symmetry. Compare probe subspaces across source languages (cosine/CCA) to test for a common low-rank certainty direction. 4) Known-but-unexpressed gap: restrict to (fact,language) pairs answered WRONG at the surface. For each, (a) apply logit-lens across layers and PatchScopes to decode intermediate states and check whether the correct object appears among top-k in ANY intermediate layer (in any language), and (b) check whether the shared certainty probe predicts 'known'. Report the fraction of wrong answers that are recoverable/known, broken down by language and by typological/script distance (URIEL). 5) Contrast with genuine gaps: verify that facts the model fails in ALL languages (true gaps) do NOT show recoverable intermediate answers, validating the distinction. 6) Training-free repair: define a language-alignment vector (difference-of-means between target-language and source-language activations on parallel content) and steer at mid layers, optionally combined with amplifying the shared certainty direction; measure accuracy recovery on known-but-unexpressed items and specificity (no gain fabricated on true-gap items, no degradation on already-correct items or on a held-out set). 7) Ablations: layer selection, probe rank, steering strength, PatchScopes vs. logit-lens agreement, and robustness across the four models. Metrics: cross-lingual probe AUC and transfer gap, known-but-unexpressed fraction, distance correlation (Spearman), repair accuracy delta, specificity/false-recovery rate, and calibration (ECE) before/after.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Logit-lens/PatchScopes decoding is noisy and may over- or under-count 'recoverable' answers; we cross-validate the two methods, require top-k agreement, and validate on known-answer control tasks. 2) The certainty probe may partly encode surface confidence rather than true 'knowing'; we control by including surface-confidence as a feature/baseline and testing incremental predictive power. 3) Popularity/frequency confounds correctness; we include popularity covariates and stratify. 4) Difference-of-means alignment vectors may entangle content and language; we use parallel translations to control content and include a language-only baseline. 5) A null result (certainty is language-specific, or the known-but-unexpressed gap is small) would still be a clean, informative finding that sharpens the knowledge-gap-vs-access debate. 6) Effects may be model-specific; we report across four models. 7) Multi-token entity answers complicate decoding; we use first-token/normalized matching with manual validation on a subset.
